title: Stones, Light and a Bold Claim
overview: A woman is spared from stoning, and then a rising argument in the temple over who Jesus is ends with his hearers picking up stones against him.

parts.label: A woman used as a trap (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: This story (7:53 to 8:11) is missing from the oldest surviving copies of John, so many scholars think it was added later, perhaps from an early memory of Jesus, though the churches still accept it as Scripture. Moses' law called for both lovers to die (Leviticus 20:10), yet only the woman is brought, as bait to force Jesus to choose between that law and his reputation for mercy.

parts.label: No one throws a stone (vv. 7-11)
parts.note: The law had the witnesses throw the first stone (Deuteronomy 17:7), so Jesus says only someone without sin should start, and no one knows what he wrote on the ground. The accusers leave, oldest first, and he sends her away uncondemned but tells her to stop sinning; some read this as forgiveness, others as him simply refusing to act as her judge.

parts.label: The light of the world (vv. 12-20)
parts.note: Some readers connect this saying with the great lamps lit in the temple courts at the Feast of Booths from chapter 7, though John does not say the feast was still going on. When critics say his word about himself proves nothing, he answers with the law's rule that two witnesses settle a matter and names his Father as the second.

parts.label: Where I go, you cannot come (vv. 21-30)
parts.note: He warns he is leaving and that they will die in their sins unless they believe 'I am he.' Many translations add 'he', but the Greek is simply 'I am', which many readers hear as echoing how God speaks of himself in Isaiah 43:10; 'lifted up' can mean raised on a cross or raised to honor, and Christians read it as pointing to his crucifixion.

parts.label: Freedom and Abraham's children (vv. 31-47)
parts.note: To people who had just believed him, Jesus says the truth will set them free, and when they protest that they were never slaves, he says anyone who keeps sinning is a slave and true children of Abraham would not plot to kill him. The argument turns bitter when he calls the devil their father (v. 44); many scholars see this as harsh language aimed at particular opponents in a dispute among fellow Jews, and most churches now reject its later use against Jewish people.

parts.label: Before Abraham, I am (vv. 48-59)
parts.note: They call him a Samaritan, from a neighboring people many Jews saw as outsiders, and say he has a demon, while he claims Abraham looked ahead to his day and was glad. Then he says 'before Abraham was born, I am,' which many hear as echoing God's name in Exodus 3:14, and his hearers apparently take it as an insult to God, since they pick up stones before he slips away.

disagreement: Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant Christians read the 'I am' of verse 58 as Jesus claiming to have always existed as God, while some groups that reject the Trinity (God as Father, Son and Spirit), such as Jehovah's Witnesses, whose translation reads 'I have been', take it as a claim to have existed before Abraham without being God.
think: Jesus would not let a crowd use one woman's wrong to shame her. What changes for you when you picture him standing beside the person everyone else is ready to condemn?
